1: Tiny robots that swim through your body, deliver medicine exactly where it is needed, then dissolve away. The future of treatment may be smaller than a speck of dust.
3: MIT's Huggable, a robotic teddy bear, helped more than 50 hospitalized kids feel better in a Pediatrics study. Sometimes the best medicine is a warm, patient friend.
4: A prosthetic arm anchored directly to the skeleton and controlled by thought alone. Independence, restored by engineering.
5: Alphabet's Wing drones crossed 100,000 deliveries, proof that the quiet work of delivery drones is paying off. Slowly, then suddenly.
6: ISRO packed 20 satellites onto a single rocket and put them all in orbit in about 26 minutes. Efficiency at rocket scale.
7: SpaceX overtook Russia as the world's most prolific commercial launcher, reshaping who gets to space. Competition lifted the whole industry.
8: Kavya Kopparapu built an AI that diagnoses her grandfather's eye disease using a smartphone and a 3D-printed lens. A teenager, a phone, and care in action.
9: An Australian National University AI recreated a Nobel-winning physics experiment in a single hour, learning the Bose-Einstein condensate setup from scratch. Machines that learn like scientists.
10: A low-cost, low-tech soft exosuit from Harvard is helping stroke victims walk again. Gentle robotics, enormous human impact.
11: A startup's CRISPR approach to curing HIV has reported its first trial results. An old dream of medicine is being tested in the real world.
12: The mRNA miracle was decades in the making, built on years of patient, unglamorous work. Overnight success takes decades.
13: This painting robot did not replace its human coworkers, it transformed what they could do together. A story about robots that lift people up.
15: Qure.ai's AI reads chest X-rays for tuberculosis in rural India, bringing expert diagnosis where doctors are scarce. Healthcare capacity, multiplied by software.
16: An AI system can hear cardiac arrest in a 911 caller's voice, sometimes better than human dispatchers. Every second counts, and now the phone can help.
18: Translation apps are quietly dissolving language barriers, making the world a little closer every day. The internet made the world smaller; translation makes it closer.
19: Satellites with cheap cameras and big data are now measuring economies in near real time. A whole new way to see how the world is doing.
21: AI and automation are shrinking the drug discovery timeline, finding the right drug for the right patient faster. Speed that saves lives.
22: One-shot gene therapies for rare diseases have arrived, turning lifelong conditions into solvable problems. Now the fight moves to making them affordable.
23: Form Energy's iron-air battery stores power for 100 hours at a tenth of lithium's cost, using rust. The humble battery just got heroic.
24: A 20-year-old inventor built a smart wheelchair that could save lives. Youth, ingenuity, and a chair that changes everything.
25: With a severed spinal cord, he walked again after an implant bridged his injury. Medicine just did the miraculous.
26: A brain chip gave a paralyzed man control of his own hand again. Thought became movement, and independence came back with it.
27: A brain implant turned a paralyzed man's thoughts directly into words, giving him back his voice. Communication, restored from within.
28: A new drug can delay type 1 diabetes in kids, buying them a full, normal childhood. Sometimes the best gift is more time.
29: The Serum Institute's massive manufacturing scale-up became the world's best hope for enough vaccine. Scale, it turns out, is a superpower.
30: Europe's emergency workers are turning to drones as game-changers for rescues and disasters. Eyes in the sky, help on the way.
31: Gene therapy ferried healthy genes into the inner ears of deaf mice, and they could hear again. A virus doing good, for once.
32: Scientists are making a bold attempt to cure HIV with CRISPR, cutting the virus out at its genetic root. Audacious science for a historic goal.
33: The Hubble is falling, and SpaceX plus a billionaire backer are exploring a mission to lift it back up. Even our greatest telescopes deserve a second act.
34: Sesame Phone gives paralyzed users a fully hands-free smartphone, controlled by head movements. Independence, one glance at a time.
35: Ford's driverless cars passed the snow test, navigating one of driving's hardest conditions. Winter just met its match.
36: Transplant surgery got a paralyzed man walking again. In the doctor's words: this is just fantastic.
37: A $70,000 exoskeleton is helping paralyzed people walk, and it is already approved in the US and the EU. Bionic legs, now real and available.
